newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean banks set Jinro bail-out at $90 million.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean banks set Jinro bail-out at $90 million.

text.p: A committee of South Korean banks on Monday agreed to extend 80.4 billion won ($90 million) in emergency loans to the troubled Jinro Group to bail out six affiliates.
The emergency loans would be made "as soon as possible", a committee official said. Jinro had sought 500 billion won.

The official of the Commercial Bank of Korea said the loans would be supplied after Jinro Group chairman Chang Jin-ho issues a letter granting banks authority to dispose of his family's shareholding in group affiliates.
It was not clear whether Chang had already agreed to give up his family's ownership and management rights in the group.
An earlier decision by the bank committee to defer debt payments for the six core affiliates of the group will be in effect until July 21, the official told reporters after the committee meeting.
The 19th-ranked Jinro Group buckled this month under 3.2 trillion won in debt, mostly a result of reckless expansion.
The group has said it would sell part of its property and affiliates to raise an estimated 1.2 trillion won by the end of 1998 for debt repayment.
The group's flagship and the nation's largest distilled liquor maker, Jinro Ltd, will get 25.1 billion won of the planned emergency loans, the official said.
Earlier on Monday, South Korea's 30 merchant banks said they had agreed to join the committee after commercial banks accepted their demand to exempt them from offering additional credit.
"We have agreed to cooperate with the commercial banks and abide by the committee's decisions," said a director of the Merchant Banks Association of Korea. He declined to be named.
Participation of the merchant banks removed a major obstacle to rescuing the stricken group, analysts said.

"An important point has now been passed in the crisis," said Namuh Rhee, head of research at Dongbang Peregrine Securities. "Jinro will now be able to get an emergency cash infusion until its asset fire-sale plan begins making money."
Jinro has said it will sell property and affiliates to raise cash to pay its debts, estimated at 3.2 trillion won.
The group has estimated the asset sale would raise about 1.2 trillion won by the end of 1998.
The group's prime creditor bank, the Commercial Bank of Korea, earlier designated the flagship Jinro Ltd and five other affiliates for the bail-out.
At the end of 1996, the six firms accounted for 80.7 percent of the group's total sales turnover and 90 percent of total assets, according to data released by the Commercial Bank.

With the country still reeling from the collapse of Hanbo Steel Co in January and Sammi Steel Co in March, the government last week said it would set up a 1.5 trillion won fund to buy, repackage and sell banks' bad debts.

Analysts said the government worried that a third high-profile bankruptcy would reveal the weakness of the country's banking system that could affect the ruling party's chances in December's presidential election.

"I think the Korean authorities are actually more worried about what happens in the commercial banking system than they are with one manufacturing company," said Graham Courtney, director of Asian economics at SBC Warburg in Tokyo.
